lessons.title: Shelter a rigorous lesson: dual goals, interaction and fading
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL UNOFFICIAL LEARNING MODULE - PARTIAL OBJECTIVE 0007

These original synthetic classroom situations are derived instruction, not official exam items or a complete SEI protocol. S1-S10 refer to this slice's supplied evidence packet, retrieved by the researcher on 2026-11-08. Codex did not retrieve the documents. The source inventory records this slice's short supporting excerpts. Model wording comparison is not human review.

CONTENT GOAL: Given a proposed grade-level lesson, preserve its reasoning target and justify a sequence of access supports, structured interaction and an evidence-based fading decision. LANGUAGE GOAL: Explain the plan using a content-and-language objective pair and causal language linking each support to a specific language demand. Observable success means the plan identifies what learners will reason about, what language they will use, what the teacher will observe and why a support changes.

STAGE 1 - Name two goals before choosing an activity.
A content goal describes disciplinary learning, such as comparing explanations of how a local habitat changed using observations. A language goal names language used to do that work: orally justify a proposed cause with an observation and a qualifying phrase, then write the reasoning. 'Learn vocabulary' alone does not specify the content relationship or the language function. S1 names concurrent objectives; S4 calls for subject frameworks and WIDA standards in tandem. The objective pair is an authored illustration, not an official WIDA performance indicator. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

STAGE 2 - Scaffold up to the content target.
Comprehensible input can include a labeled image, a brief demonstration, chunked directions and an organizer that makes a relation visible. Invite useful familiar-language notes or discussion and check what meaning they contribute; no language background guarantees a particular strategy. A scaffold changes access to the same reasoning. Replacing a causal investigation with naming easy objects removes the target. WIDA protects complex texts, rigorous learning and meaningful discussion; a proficiency description cannot justify below-grade content 'because EL.' [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S3 source.obj0004-0006.s3.2026-11-08]

STAGE 3 - Make interaction intellectually consequential.
After a teacher thinks aloud about one observation, partners choose between explanations, point to evidence, ask a clarifying question and revise a claim. A rotating listener role must paraphrase the reasoning before disagreeing. Give preparation time and optional visual or multilingual notes. These concrete routines are authored applications of S1 interaction, S2 active engagement and S5/S6 content talk, not a proprietary feature list. The WWC anchors concern elementary/middle-grade instruction; this lesson's grade 6 example stays within that scope. A silent worksheet after a lecture may provide input but cannot alone demonstrate meaningful academic interaction. Make disagreement about an interpretation safe by inviting revision and evaluating evidence rather than accent or speed. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S5 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08] [S6 source.obj0004-0006.s6.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - Preserve the comparison while opening access.
A grade 6 class compares two synthetic wetland observations: one area has dense plant cover and clearer water; another has sparse cover and murkier water. The content goal is to propose and qualify an explanation, including the limit that two observations alone do not establish cause. The language goal is to connect a claim and observation with 'because' and qualify it with 'may' or an equivalent expression. First show the locations and label only the words needed to discuss the comparison. Model the distinction between an observation and an explanation. Partners use an observation/claim/uncertainty organizer, ask what other evidence could matter, then write. This preserves reasoning and gives language a real purpose. A counterproposal asks ELs only to copy 'plant' and 'water' while classmates evaluate causation. It removes the target and supplies no evidence that those learners cannot reason about causes. [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 1 - Assisted rehearsal; no attempts or independent evidence.
Read the example with the explanation visible. Which change keeps the content goal: add a labeled diagram and partner rehearsal, or replace causal comparison with matching nouns? Pause and explain using 'The support changes ___ while the target remains ___.' Assisted comparison: the diagram and rehearsal preserve the causal comparison; matching alone replaces it. A learner may still need explicit word instruction, but that instruction prepares access to reasoning rather than substituting for it. Nothing typed or said here is recorded as an attempt or evidence; later unaided checks are separate.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - Coordinate SCI and ESL, then test a fading decision.
In a grade 7 civic-history lesson, students compare two explanations of a public-space change. The content teacher and ESL teacher co-plan by jointly examining the text, identify cause-and-contrast language, and plan different observations of the same function. Sheltered Content Instruction (SCI) integrates language development with grade-level content throughout the day. Dedicated ESL provides focused language instruction; accessible content alone does not replace it. Scheduling ESL during the core history investigation would remove the very content opportunity the support should help students access. S4 instead protects core SEI content and calls for common planning time and collective responsibility. [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

The team first offers a contrast frame and source organizer. Later, after students explain a comparison without reading the frame in more than one classroom opportunity, it invites a new comparison with an optional frame. The teacher checks whether evidence and contrast remain clear. If reasoning or expression breaks down, restore or revise the support and investigate the demand; do not label the learner. This is an authored monitoring plan, not a mandated schedule or score threshold. Keeping every support forever without checking need can obscure independence; removing them solely because a calendar says so is equally unjustified. S10's annual review concerns assessment accommodations. It supports review of need but does not dictate a classroom frame-removal timetable or permission to remove an authorized testing accommodation. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0007-0009.s10.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 2 - Assisted comparison; no attempts or independent evidence.
A team says: 'The ESL teacher will fix English elsewhere; the content teacher can plan alone.' With the source explanation visible, identify the missing planning action. Assisted response: jointly identify the lesson's language demands, preserve dedicated ESL and core content time, and agree what observations will guide support changes. Shared responsibility requires an instructional connection, not merely exchanging a student's proficiency label. Your rehearsal remains assisted; it is not independent practice evidence.

STAGE 4 - Check the plan and its limits.
Ask whether the learner still investigates the same disciplinary question, uses language for that question, interacts with others about evidence and has a later opportunity to show reduced need for a support. Observe the actual response and revise. Do not infer ability, disability, culture traits or trauma from language background. This partial lesson does not supply full SEI programming models, proprietary SIOP features, model performance-indicator tables or a complete classroom-management system. Those remain gaps; no objective is complete.

lessons.title: Academic language: analyze meaning from words to discourse
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL UNOFFICIAL LEARNING MODULE - PARTIAL OBJECTIVE 0008

All texts, learners and teaching moves below are original synthetic illustrations. This is not an official examination prompt, a full disciplinary language progression or a diagnostic instrument. S1-S10 identify the supplied researcher packet; Codex did not retrieve the documents. Model comparison of source wording is not human review or evidence of learner mastery.

CONTENT GOAL: Analyze a short disciplinary text and preserve its claim, evidence, causal relations and uncertainty when designing instruction. LANGUAGE GOAL: Identify a word/phrase demand, a sentence relationship and a discourse relationship; explain how a support helps learners interpret and produce meaning at each dimension. Observable success includes an annotated text, a justified teaching sequence and an original evidence-based response beyond a filled frame.

STAGE 1 - Start with the communicative task, not a fluency label.
Comfortable social conversation can coexist with difficulty interpreting a dense source or justifying a claim in writing. That observation identifies an instructional question; it does not prove inability, readiness or a disability. Social and academic language overlap in real use, and the distinction does not establish a fixed acquisition calendar. Look at what the learner is being asked to understand and produce in this discipline. S1 explicitly includes strong social but limited academic language; S2 identifies language dimensions without turning proficiency snapshots into student labels. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

STAGE 2 - Analyze three connected dimensions.
At the word/phrase dimension, check everyday words used in a special sense, cross-disciplinary words such as 'evidence' or 'consequence,' technical terms and dense noun groups. At the sentence dimension, ask who acts, what changes, which clauses express cause, contrast or qualification, and what pronouns refer to. At discourse dimension, ask how a whole passage builds meaning: what question it answers, how claims and evidence connect, what information is assumed, and how cohesion and density affect understanding. WIDA 2020 supplies discourse, sentence and word/phrase dimensions. Calling every difficulty 'vocabulary' can leave the causal structure invisible. [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - Read a sentence as an argument, not a word list.
Original grade 7 science text: 'Although the upstream channel remained clear, sediment carried from the exposed bank after rainfall reduced light downstream. This change may help explain the fewer submerged plants, but the observations do not rule out other causes.' First establish the content question: what explanation is supported and how certain is it? At word/phrase level, unpack 'sediment carried from the exposed bank' into material, origin and movement; distinguish everyday 'clear' from this water context. At sentence level, draw arrows from rainfall to movement and from sediment to reduced light; explain that 'although' contrasts locations and 'may' qualifies the inference. At discourse level, connect 'This change' to reduced light and compare the proposed cause with the stated limit. The text does not prove a single cause. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

The teacher models the first clause, then pairs reconstruct the relation using a diagram and explain why a second interpretation would need more evidence. A vocabulary-only counterexample preteaches twenty isolated words and asks students to repeat the paragraph. Even accurate definitions would not show what 'This change' refers to or why the conclusion is qualified. Vocabulary instruction remains valuable, but it must serve comprehension. S5 supports intensive instruction in a selected academic word set across several days and integration of oral and written language with content; it does not prescribe twenty random words. [S5 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 1 - Assisted text analysis; no attempts or independent evidence.
Keep the worked analysis visible. Does 'may' change the proposed event or the writer's certainty about its explanation? Assisted comparison: it qualifies the explanatory claim; deleting it can overstate what the observations establish. Identify the word-level, sentence-level and discourse-level work that supports that interpretation. The demonstration answer is present, so this rehearsal produces no attempts or independent evidence.

STAGE 3 - Teach forms as choices that serve meaning.
Offer a frame such as 'The observation ___ supports ___ because ___; however, ___ remains uncertain.' Model one use, compare it with a misleading use, and invite a different wording that preserves the relationship. A frame can reduce the burden of organizing English while learners reason. It does not supply the evidence, decide whether a claim follows or replace participation in an authentic argument. Students should question a partner's warrant, revise a claim and choose wording for an audience. S4 names arguing with evidence and justifying conclusions; S1 includes frames and inclusion in academic discourse. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - Fluent conversation, new disciplinary discourse.
A grade 8 history group readily discusses weekend activities but writes, 'The council changed the rule. People complained. It was bad.' Its sources show a complaint before the change and a budget note mentioning a separate concern. The content goal is to compare explanations without claiming that sequence proves causation. The language goal is to link each explanation to a source, contrast the evidence and qualify certainty. Teach a small useful word set ('claim,' 'evidence,' 'constraint') in context, unpack a sentence with two possible causes, and jointly map claim-evidence-limitation relations. Partners then argue for one interpretation, listen to a competing explanation and revise their written conclusion. The teacher observes the reasoning and language separately. Strong conversational English does not eliminate the need for this instruction. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08] [S5 source.obj0004-0006.s5.2026-11-08]

A counterproposal has students insert 'because' into every sentence, then awards full argument credit. It checks completion of a structure while leaving the source reasoning unexamined. Another uses a frame that says 'The only cause was ___'; that frame actually forces an unsupported conclusion. An appropriate frame leaves room to qualify or disagree. As learners express the relationships with less assistance, offer the frame as optional and assess a fresh source comparison. This classroom sequence is an authored application, not an effect-size claim or a fixed language-development timetable.

GUIDED CHECK 2 - Assisted comparison; no attempts or evidence.
Which response better meets the goals: a fully completed frame with no source, or a shorter explanation that identifies evidence and limits but needs a language revision? Assisted answer: examine the second response's disciplinary reasoning and teach the needed form, while checking the first for unsupported claims. A frame is a support, not proof of understanding. Use this visible answer for rehearsal only; it does not create independent evidence.

STAGE 4 - Transfer the analysis cautiously.
The same dimension questions apply across subjects, but the actual language demand differs. A mathematics comparison may hinge on a conditional relationship; science may distinguish a mechanism from a correlation; history may attribute a claim to a source; language arts may justify an interpretation using narrative details. These are original examples, not official disciplinary taxonomies. Select the text and purpose first, then identify its particular demands. Use visuals, familiar-language planning and structured talk when useful without predicting strategies from nationality. WWC guidance used here is scoped to elementary and middle grades; it is not proof of identical effects at every age. This partial slice leaves complete subject progressions, detailed literacy/disability-specific interventions and broad Massachusetts framework analysis as gaps. No objective is complete.

lessons.title: Assessment decisions: domains, access and uncertainty
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL UNOFFICIAL LEARNING MODULE - PARTIAL OBJECTIVE 0009

Every profile and classroom observation below is synthetic. None is a private learner record, official item or reclassification decision. This derived lesson compares wording with the supplied packet; Codex did not retrieve documents or independently verify binary hashes. Source-checked model comparison is not human review. It cannot determine an individual's eligibility, disability or testing accommodations.

CONTENT GOAL: Given a language profile and classroom evidence, distinguish the construct being assessed, preserve the content target, choose an access or monitoring action and state what remains uncertain. LANGUAGE GOAL: Justify the decision with domain-specific observations and qualified claims using 'suggests,' 'does not establish' and a reasoned next step. Observable success means naming the evidence, the bounded inference and an additional observation that could change the plan.

STAGE 1 - Identify the assessment purpose.
An English language proficiency assessment concerns English language use; a classroom content task concerns a disciplinary target. ACCESS supplies English language proficiency evidence by Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing. It is not a measure of mathematics understanding, content ability, readiness or disability, and its results are not student labels. MCAS concerns content achievement with applicable accessibility rules. A teacher must still inspect the actual task and score interpretation. Do not use a language result as a substitute for a content assessment. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]

STAGE 2 - Inspect domains and measurement uncertainty.
An Overall composite can hide differences: stronger performance in one domain can raise the composite while another needs attention. Inspect all four domains and the classroom language demands, not Overall alone. S9 says proficiency levels are domain specific and equal scale scores across domains are not interchangeable. A scale score is one point in a range of possible performance, represented by confidence bands using Standard Error of Measurement (SEM). A single administration therefore supports cautious interpretation and triangulation, not certainty about every future task. The supplied guide also treats 2025-2026 ACCESS scale scores as a new baseline; do not compare these scale scores with previous-year scale scores. No score-conversion formula, growth threshold or numerical exit rule is taught here. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - An uneven profile does not answer a content question.
A synthetic grade 6 learner has stronger Listening and Speaking evidence than Reading and Writing evidence. The learner correctly sorts photographs of material changes and orally explains why one change may be reversible, but a dense written worksheet is incomplete. The Overall result alone cannot tell the teacher which language demand caused difficulty. First inspect the domains, then compare the reading load with the task. Use the same science criterion in a labeled-diagram explanation with brief oral follow-up, while separately examining how the learner reads the written directions and expresses a justification. This may reveal content understanding alongside a language instructional need; it does not automatically prove either. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]

Counterexample: 'Low ACCESS Reading means low science ability, so remove the explanation target.' The inference substitutes one construct for another and lowers expectations without content evidence. Another counterexample declares all supports unnecessary because Overall looks strong. It erases the domain difference and the classroom observations. A better next step targets the written explanation language while preserving the science reasoning, then checks a new task with less help when appropriate. Neither one good diagram nor one weak worksheet establishes comprehensive mastery. [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 1 - Assisted interpretation; no attempts or independent evidence.
With the analysis visible, name two things the teacher should inspect before changing the plan. Assisted answer: domain-specific English language evidence and performance on the same content target with reduced irrelevant language load. A plausible additional check might separate comprehension of a direction from understanding the science relation. This rehearsal records no attempts or independent evidence; it does not create a student assessment record.

STAGE 3 - Preserve the construct while improving access.
For a formative science check, a labeled diagram plus oral explanation can reduce writing burden while retaining a causal explanation criterion. If the target itself is written argument, however, removing all writing changes what is being observed; collect content and written-language evidence separately. Linguistic and cultural bias can arise when an irrelevant language demand or assumed background knowledge obscures the intended construct. Examine the actual materials and opportunities; never attribute a bias pattern or a cultural trait to an individual from their language background. S1 calls for valid assessment and lower linguistic load with high content expectations. This brief example does not validate an instrument psychometrically. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - Access support, routine use and a timely evaluation.
A synthetic grade 7 learner routinely uses a familiar bilingual glossary to interpret directions in a civics unit and still compares competing arguments using the same evidence criterion as peers. That classroom support addresses language access. A proposal to remove the comparison standard and grade only word matching would modify the learning target. S10 says EL accommodations address English-language barriers, should not appear only on test day and should be examined annually as proficiency grows. It warns against unfamiliar bilingual dictionaries/glossaries. Its explicit no-lowered-expectations quotation occurs in the disability section; S1 independently preserves high content expectations for EL assessment. Classroom use alone does not authorize a particular MCAS support: check current tables and applicable individual rules for an actual state test. This lesson supplies no accommodation codes. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0007-0009.s10.2026-11-08]

Now add persistent difficulties across well-supported classroom opportunities and a reason for the team to suspect a disability. EL status is neither evidence of disability nor a reason to postpone a warranted special education evaluation until English is fluent. Continue appropriate language support and culturally and linguistically appropriate, domain-aware progress monitoring while following the warranted evaluation process. Do not diagnose from the ACCESS result, and do not require a fixed period of language intervention before considering evaluation. The packet supplies neither an evaluation timeline nor a diagnosis. [S7 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]

GUIDED CHECK 2 - Assisted comparison; no attempts or evidence.
A colleague proposes waiting for fluent English before investigating the documented concern. Explain why that reasoning fails without claiming the student has a disability. Assisted answer: S7 rejects delay based solely on EL status when there is reason to suspect disability; the team should pursue a warranted evaluation with appropriate evidence and language access. The existence of concern justifies investigation, not a predetermined conclusion. This visible explanation is assisted rehearsal only.

STAGE 4 - Make the next step conditional and observable.
Record the construct, domain evidence, supports already used, content observations and uncertainty. Specify what a new observation would clarify and what result would prompt a support revision or consultation. Use SEM humility: a point score from one administration is not an exact boundary between instructional identities. Triangulate without inventing a numeric decision rule. Review access supports as need changes, and preserve required procedures. Never infer ability, disability, culture traits or trauma from language background. Remaining gaps include full psychometrics, instrument validation, exhaustive assessment/rubric design, current MCAS code tables, individual eligibility and numeric Massachusetts exit/reclassification criteria. These cases do not mark any objective complete.

tasks.title: Align two goals to one investigation
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. A grade 6 team plans a lesson in which students compare two explanations of a habitat change using observations. Which objective pair best preserves both content learning and purposeful language development?

options.text: Learn the names of six organisms and complete an English word-search instead of comparing explanations.
Compare explanations using observations; orally justify a claim with evidence and a qualifying phrase, then write the reasoning.
Use because in five sentences, regardless of whether the statements explain the habitat observations.
Compare explanations, but postpone all attention to language until the content unit ends.

answerKey.feedback: The pair keeps the disciplinary comparison and names language used to justify and qualify it. S1 specifies concurrent content/language objectives; S4 teaches content frameworks and WIDA standards in tandem. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Naming organisms may prepare access, but the word-search replaces the explanation target. S1 requires concurrent objectives and S4 preserves grade-level content with academic language. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: A connective alone does not define a meaningful language objective aligned to the investigation. S4 pairs standards and academic practices such as justifying conclusions, not disconnected form counts. [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: The disciplinary comparison is appropriate, but delaying all language planning misses the concurrent instruction S1 and S4 describe. The needed explanatory language belongs in this lesson. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Open access without replacing the problem
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. In a grade-level mathematics lesson, students compare two solution strategies and explain why both work. A learner needs help interpreting the directions. Which initial response preserves the target?

options.text: Assign below-grade addition facts because the learner is an EL.
Let the learner watch others compare strategies but require no explanation.
Remove the comparison and ask only for the final answer.
Clarify directions with a diagram and useful familiar-language notes, then structure partner explanation of the same strategies.

answerKey.feedback: The support changes language access while retaining comparison and explanation. WIDA calls for access to grade-level content and forbids using proficiency descriptions to restrict rigorous participation. [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: EL status does not establish a need for below-grade content. WIDA protects rigorous grade-level access; the observed difficulty concerns directions, not demonstrated mathematical understanding. [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: Observation can prepare participation, but eliminating the learner's explanation removes an opportunity to do the reasoning. WIDA includes active engagement and meaningful discussion. [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: A final answer alone omits the specified comparison. S1 differentiates access while maintaining high content expectations; deleting the reasoning target does not satisfy that boundary. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Let evidence guide a support change
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. During a history unit, several classroom observations show a learner can connect source evidence to a claim without reading the offered sentence frame. What is the most defensible next instructional step?

options.text: Offer a fresh comparable task with the frame optional, observe whether the relationship stays clear, and restore or revise support if needed.
Require the identical frame permanently because EL status always means it is necessary.
Remove every classroom and testing support immediately because one frame is less needed.
Wait a fixed number of months before looking at any evidence of independent expression.

answerKey.feedback: Use observed performance to try a bounded reduction while preserving the target and monitoring the result. This is an authored classroom application; S10 supports review as proficiency grows but does not prescribe a classroom timetable or authorize wholesale testing changes. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0007-0009.s10.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.b: Permanent assignment without checking need ignores the evidence in the scenario. S10 calls for review as proficiency grows; it does not make EL status proof that every support must remain unchanged. [S10 source.obj0007-0009.s10.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: Evidence about one classroom frame does not justify removing all supports or authorized testing accommodations. S10 requires considered review of accessibility needs, not blanket removal. [S10 source.obj0007-0009.s10.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: The supplied sources provide no fixed classroom fading calendar. S1 emphasizes access with high expectations, and S10 supports reviewing supports as proficiency develops. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0007-0009.s10.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Preserve both core content and dedicated ESL
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. A school offers sheltered grade-level science and a dedicated ESL block. A proposed timetable puts ESL during the science investigation because the science teacher already uses visuals. Which revision best fits the supplied SEI guidance?

options.text: Cancel ESL because visuals in science supply all needed dedicated language instruction.
Keep the conflict because missing core science is the intended role of ESL.
Protect both core sheltered science and dedicated ESL, coordinating their language purposes without removing learners from core content.
Replace both lessons with a general English worksheet period.

answerKey.feedback: SCI integrates grade-level content and academic language, while dedicated ESL provides focused language instruction. The guidance explicitly says not to remove ELs from core SEI content for ESL. [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Visual access in SCI does not replace the dedicated focus of ESL. The guidance distinguishes the roles and says content accessibility alone is insufficient. [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: This reverses the guidance: schools should not remove EL students from core SEI content to participate in ESL. The timetable must preserve access to both. [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: A general worksheet period discards the grade-level content and focused language functions. S4 pairs content and WIDA standards while retaining distinct, coordinated instruction. [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Make shared planning change the lesson
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. A content teacher prepares a civic debate while the ESL teacher teaches a separate vocabulary list. Students cannot connect source evidence to their claims. Which next planning action addresses the mismatch?

options.text: Ask the ESL teacher to correct every grammar error after the debate without seeing the content sources.
Jointly inspect the sources, identify evidence/qualification language, align goals and agree what classroom observations will guide supports.
Have the content teacher send only the Overall ACCESS result and then plan alone.
Delete the debate so neither teacher needs to coordinate language demands.

answerKey.feedback: Common planning connects language demands, content reasoning and observations. S4 calls for common planning time and collective responsibility; S1 identifies the SEI teacher's partnership with ESL staff. [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08] [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Correction after the event does not resolve the unplanned evidence-language demand. S4's shared planning and concurrent standards call for coordinated instruction, not a correction handoff. [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: A composite result does not analyze the debate text or align the two teachers' goals. S4 requires collaboration; S9 also cautions that composite scores can conceal domain differences. [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Deleting the debate removes the challenging opportunity rather than making it accessible. S1 explicitly links collaboration to comprehensive, challenging educational opportunities. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Plan beyond conversational fluency
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. A grade 8 learner chats fluently with classmates but gives a source-based history explanation with no link between claim and evidence. Which response best addresses the observation?

options.text: Treat conversational fluency as proof that academic language instruction is unnecessary.
Assign only basic greetings because any weak academic response shows no useful English.
Wait for a universal academic-language acquisition deadline before teaching the relationship.
Teach and rehearse how disciplinary claims connect to evidence, while checking the learner's content interpretation and preserving the source task.

answerKey.feedback: S1 explicitly distinguishes strong social language from limited academic language. Instruction should address the task's discourse demand; S4 identifies arguing with evidence and justifying conclusions as academic practices. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S4 source.obj0004-0006.s7.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Social ease does not establish proficiency for every disciplinary language purpose. S1 specifically names learners whose strong social language coexists with academic-language needs. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: The observation concerns one academic relation, not an absence of useful language or content capacity. WIDA language descriptions do not categorize a learner or justify restricting rigorous materials. [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: The supplied sources do not give a fixed acquisition calendar for this decision. S1 calls for planning around actual academic-language needs, and WIDA performance depends on context. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Analyze how a dense text makes meaning
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. A science passage reads: "Although the covered soil retained moisture, water loss from the exposed soil after heating increased. This difference may reflect the covering, but another factor could contribute." Before teaching, what analysis most directly supports comprehension?

options.text: Unpack the dense noun group, track the contrast and the referent of This difference, and examine how may qualifies the whole explanation.
Choose twenty unfamiliar-looking words without reading the sentence or considering the explanation.
Remove although and may because those words cannot affect scientific meaning.
Count the sentence lengths and assume that shorter sentences always preserve the argument.

answerKey.feedback: The analysis joins word/phrase, sentence and discourse work: the event named by a noun group, clause relations, cohesion and a qualified explanatory claim. S1 specifies meaning-based analysis; WIDA supplies the three dimensions. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.b: A disconnected word list can miss what the clauses and references mean together. S1 names rhetorical structure and clause-by-clause analysis, and S2 distinguishes dimensions beyond vocabulary. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: Although marks contrast and may marks uncertainty in this authored passage. Removing them can change the claim, contrary to S1's meaning-based analysis of demanding language. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Length alone cannot show whether a contrast, causal relation or qualification remains. S2's discourse dimension concerns overall meaning and cohesion, not a universal sentence-length rule. [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Separate English reading from mathematical reasoning
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. A learner's synthetic ACCESS Reading result is lower than the Listening result. A teacher wants to use Reading to place the learner in a lower mathematics ability group before seeing any mathematics work. What is the sound response?

options.text: Use the lower domain as a direct mathematics ability score.
Average Reading and Listening to create a mathematics readiness score.
Reject that inference; inspect the mathematics target and collect content evidence with appropriate language access while planning for the reading demand.
Use Listening alone to decide that all mathematics and language support is unnecessary.

answerKey.feedback: ACCESS domain scores concern English language proficiency, not mathematics understanding, readiness or ability. S9 requires domain-specific interpretation; S1 supports content checks with reduced linguistic load and high expectations. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08] [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: The Reading domain measures English language proficiency in that domain; it cannot establish mathematics ability. WIDA also lists cognitive ability and readiness among inappropriate proficiency-description uses. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: Combining language scores does not change the construct into mathematics readiness. S9 warns against treating domain measures interchangeably, and S2 rejects readiness inferences from language descriptions. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: A stronger Listening result does not establish every content or language need. S9 favors inspecting domains; content understanding still requires relevant classroom evidence. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Inspect what the composite hides
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. Two synthetic ACCESS profiles have the same reported Overall result. One has stronger Listening and Speaking with weaker Reading and Writing; the other is more even. A colleague proposes identical support removal based solely on Overall. Which response is best?

options.text: Proceed because equal composites guarantee identical language needs.
Inspect all four domains and classroom demands, target the differing literacy needs, and keep current exit-policy decisions separate from this instructional comparison.
Use only the strongest domain to define each learner's permanent language level.
Treat the weaker literacy domains as evidence of low content ability or disability.

answerKey.feedback: A stronger domain can inflate a composite, masking different profiles. S9 says individual domain performance is more informative than one composite; classroom evidence helps plan the relevant reading/writing language instruction. No exit threshold follows. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Equal Overall results can conceal different language portraits. S9 explicitly cautions that composites need careful consideration and directs attention to individual domains. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: One strong domain does not describe every language purpose and is not a permanent learner label. S9 requires domain-aware interpretation and S2 treats proficiency as a snapshot. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08] [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Language proficiency does not establish cognitive/content ability or disability. S2 excludes those inferences and S7 says EL status itself is not a basis for a disability determination. [S2 source.obj0004-0006.s2.2026-11-08] [S7 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Keep the science criterion visible
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. The formative goal is explaining why a material changes when heated, not producing an extended written essay. A learner has difficulty with the essay directions. Which check best preserves the intended content evidence?

options.text: Grade isolated vocabulary definitions as the entire science explanation.
Award full science understanding solely for completing the worksheet.
Remove the causal explanation target and ask only for a drawing of the equipment.
Ask for a labeled diagram plus oral causal explanation, using the same science criterion and recording the separate language observations.

answerKey.feedback: The check reduces an incidental writing burden while retaining causal explanation. S1 explicitly describes lower linguistic load with high content expectations and using informal results to inform instruction. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Vocabulary definitions alone do not show the targeted causal reasoning. S1 links formative assessment to the intended content purpose while preserving expectations. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: Completion is not evidence of the specified understanding. S1 emphasizes interpreting formative results to inform instruction, which requires examining the actual explanation. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: Drawing equipment without explaining the change omits the target. S1 permits changes to linguistic load while maintaining high content and knowledge expectations. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Distinguish language access from a changed standard
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. For a classroom civics assessment of comparing arguments, a learner routinely uses a familiar bilingual glossary. A team also proposes removing the comparison goal. Which judgment is best supported?

options.text: The glossary can support classroom access while preserving comparison; removing the goal changes expectations. Check current MCAS rules separately before any state-test use and review support needs over time.
Both changes preserve the same construct because any easier task is an accommodation.
Introduce an unfamiliar glossary only on the state-test day, without classroom practice or eligibility review.
Retain every support permanently without reviewing proficiency or task demands.

answerKey.feedback: S1 preserves high content expectations. S10 says EL supports address language barriers, require routine use and annual review, and warns against unfamiliar glossaries. The classroom example does not establish MCAS authorization. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08] [S10 source.obj0007-0009.s10.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.b: Removing comparison changes the learning target; easier content is not merely improved language access. S1 explicitly maintains high content expectations when reducing linguistic load. [S1 source.obj0007-0009.s1.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: S10 says accommodations should not be used solely for testing and discourages unfamiliar bilingual dictionaries/glossaries. Actual state-test use also requires applicable current rules. [S10 source.obj0007-0009.s10.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: S10 calls for examining and revising supports annually as English proficiency grows. Review should consider evidence of need; EL status does not require unchanged supports indefinitely. [S10 source.obj0007-0009.s10.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Investigate a concern without a language gate
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. A synthetic team has documented persistent concerns across linguistically appropriate, supported classroom observations and has reason to suspect a disability. A colleague says evaluation must wait until English is fluent. Which response fits the supplied guidance?

options.text: Agree: EL status makes a warranted evaluation inappropriate until fluency.
Diagnose a disability from EL status without evaluating the concern.
Continue appropriate language support and domain-aware monitoring while pursuing the warranted evaluation; EL status neither proves disability nor justifies delay.
Replace the observations with the Overall ACCESS result as the sole diagnostic evidence.

answerKey.feedback: S7 rejects both determining disability from EL status and delaying evaluation because of that status when disability is suspected. Its monitoring guidance is culturally/linguistically appropriate and attentive to domains; no diagnosis or timeline is inferred. [S7 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: This is the delay S7 explicitly rejects when there is reason to suspect disability. English fluency is not a prerequisite for a warranted evaluation. [S7 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: S7 says EL status is not itself a basis for determining disability. A concern calls for appropriate evaluation and evidence, not a predetermined diagnosis. [S7 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: A composite English proficiency result cannot diagnose disability. S9 warns that composites conceal domain variation; S7 rejects disability determination based on EL status. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08] [S7 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Interpret a point score with measurement humility
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice, not an official examination item. A team proposes removing a support after one ACCESS administration because the point score looks higher. It has not examined confidence bands, domains or classroom work. What is the best next step?

options.text: Treat the point score as exact proof that every related language demand is now independent.
Inspect domain results and SEM confidence bands, triangulate classroom observations, and make a bounded support decision with remaining uncertainty stated.
Discard all language results because measurement error makes every observation useless.
Compare equal scale-score numbers across different domains as if they represent the same proficiency, ignoring the guide's interpretive cautions.

answerKey.feedback: S9 explains that a scale score is one point in a range of possible performance and that domains are distinct. Confidence-band humility supports triangulation, not automatic support removal or dismissal of evidence. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: S9 explicitly uses SEM confidence bands to remind readers that a scale score is not an exact description of all possible performance. One administration alone does not establish every instructional need. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: Uncertainty calls for careful interpretation, not discarding evidence. S9 provides domain and confidence-band guidance to make results more informative alongside other observations. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: S9 says scale scores may be compared across grades but not treated interchangeably across domains. Equal numbers do not establish equal proficiency in different domains. [S9 source.obj0007-0009.s9.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Co-plan a sheltered public-exhibition investigation
tasks.prompt:
Original unfamiliar non-math application. All texts, people, scores and observations are synthetic. This is not an official examination item, official writing prompt or five-part mentor task. No deterministic answer key. The response remains needs_review and provisional/manual pending judgment.

A grade 7 class will design a small exhibition recommending how to protect a historic outdoor mural. The content target is to compare two protection proposals using evidence and acknowledge tradeoffs. Students have three original source summaries:

- An observation log describes color fading on the sun-facing panel and surface damage near a drain. It does not establish which factor caused each change.
- A transparent cover would reduce direct contact but the proposal gives no observations about moisture behind it.
- A roof extension would reduce direct rainfall on part of the mural but would leave an edge exposed and change the view from the path.

The class must recommend a next investigation before making a final design recommendation. One group can show concerns on a labeled sketch but has difficulty connecting observations to claims in a written paragraph. Another repeats the teacher's model sentence without explaining its evidence. These observations are limited; no disability or fixed language profile is given. Some learners offer familiar-language notes to help plan their arguments. A colleague suggests giving ELs only a color-matching worksheet while other students evaluate the proposals. The proposed timetable places dedicated ESL during the exhibition investigation.

You and the ESL teacher have a planning meeting. Create and justify a coherent lesson sequence:
1. State an observable content goal and a concurrent language goal aligned to a language function needed for this investigation. Identify the evidence, uncertainty and tradeoff learners must preserve. Do not invent a measured effect of either protection proposal.
2. Analyze a particular input demand and design a visual, text or familiar-language support that changes access without replacing the grade-level comparison. Explain why the color-matching alternative fails the target.
3. Design structured interaction in which students compare proposals, ask for evidence and revise. Specify what the listener must do and how learners can disagree safely without being judged by accent or speed. A teacher lecture followed by silent copying is not sufficient to demonstrate this interaction.
4. Specify what the content and ESL teachers will co-plan, what each will observe and how dedicated ESL and core SCI can both remain available. Explain why successful sheltering does not substitute for dedicated ESL and why pulling students from the core investigation is a problem.
5. Identify an initially useful scaffold and a later opportunity to observe its reduced use. State what evidence would justify making it optional, what would prompt restoration or revision and what remains uncertain. Do not invent a fixed calendar or automatic score threshold. Keep classroom fading distinct from authorization to remove a state-test accommodation.
6. Describe a brief unaided follow-up on a fresh but comparable proposal, making clear that the scaffolded lesson observations themselves are assisted. Explain how you would separate evidence of content reasoning from control of the target English forms.

Use S1's concurrent goals, interaction and partnership scope, S2's scaffold-up access, S3's language-resource principle and S4's SCI/ESL collaboration. S5/S6 support purposeful content talk in elementary/middle grades. S10 offers a bounded assessment-review analogy, not a classroom fading schedule. This case samples co-planning and responsive access; it does not establish a full SIOP protocol or comprehensive SEI-program design.

Review boundary: judge the reasoning, use of evidence, tradeoffs and uncertainty through a real human action. There is no single required plan or keyword list. Keywords, completion, an unfamiliar tag or agreement with an example establish neither an authoritative judgment nor independent transfer evidence or mastery. Source-checked content denotes model wording comparison only, not human review. Do not infer ability, disability, culture traits or trauma from language background.

tasks.title: Analyze an archive passage and teach its argument
tasks.prompt:
Original unfamiliar non-math application. All texts, people, scores and observations are synthetic. This is not an official examination item, official writing prompt or five-part mentor task. No deterministic answer key. The response remains needs_review and provisional/manual pending judgment.

A grade 8 history class is preparing an interpretation of why a neighborhood reading room changed its opening hours. The class has this original synthetic passage:

"Although the committee's adoption of shorter evening hours followed the petition, the meeting note attributes the change to staffing constraints. The petition's request for quiet on the adjacent street may have influenced discussion; however, neither document establishes that it determined the schedule. This distinction limits the claim that the petition alone caused the change."

A source card says the petition was dated before the meeting note. Neither source reports what every committee member believed, and no other record is provided. The content target is to compare competing explanations, attribute claims to sources and qualify causation. Students readily discuss neighborhood events socially. A draft says, "People asked. Then the hours changed. The petition caused it." A peer proposes adding several formal words without changing that claim. Another proposes a frame beginning, "The only reason was ___."

Analyze the text and design a short sequence that leads to authentic academic discourse:
1. Identify a defensible content claim and a limit on the available evidence. Explain why temporal sequence alone does not establish the claimed cause.
2. Annotate one dense noun group, a clause relationship and a discourse connection. Unpack who acted in "the committee's adoption"; explain what although and however connect; identify the referent and argumentative role of "This distinction." Connect each language feature to meaning, not simply a terminology label.
3. Choose a small, purposeful set of everyday/cross-disciplinary/technical word or phrase demands for this passage. Explain why merely preteaching twenty random words would miss an important sentence or discourse demand. You need not invent a fixed classification for every word.
4. Model how to unpack and reconstruct one sentence without deleting attribution or uncertainty. Supply an original short example, explaining a choice of form and its effect on the claim.
5. Offer a frame that can help express claim, evidence and qualification without deciding the answer. Explain why "The only reason was" can distort this text. Design partner argument and revision in which a learner must respond to a competing explanation rather than only complete blanks.
6. State observable content and language goals. Specify an assisted check and a later less-assisted new-passage check, describing the observations that would distinguish an evidentiary misunderstanding from needing English to express an understood relationship. Strong social conversation does not settle that distinction.

Use S1's meaning-based analysis and discourse inclusion, S2's word/phrase, sentence and discourse dimensions, S4's academic practices and S5's contextual vocabulary/content-language instruction. Do not invent a fixed social-to-academic acquisition timeline, cultural explanation or private learner profile. This case samples analysis of one text; it leaves full disciplinary progressions and individualized intervention design as gaps.

Review boundary: judge the reasoning, use of evidence, tradeoffs and uncertainty through a real human action. There is no single required plan or keyword list. Keywords, completion, an unfamiliar tag or agreement with an example establish neither an authoritative judgment nor independent transfer evidence or mastery. Source-checked content denotes model wording comparison only, not human review. Do not infer ability, disability, culture traits or trauma from language background.

tasks.title: Triangulate a language profile and classroom assessment
tasks.prompt:
Original unfamiliar non-math application. All texts, people, scores and observations are synthetic. This is not an official examination item, official writing prompt or five-part mentor task. No deterministic answer key. The response remains needs_review and provisional/manual pending judgment.

A grade 6 science team is studying how shade and watering could affect a community garden. The content target is to compare explanations for different plant growth, use observations and acknowledge that the available data do not isolate a single cause. Here is an invented ACCESS proficiency-level profile used only as a scenario: Listening 4.8, Speaking 4.2, Reading 2.7, Writing 2.3. These are synthetic domain values, not scale-score conversions, exit criteria or a real score report. No Overall composite or confidence-band endpoints are supplied. Do not calculate a composite, fabricate SEM values or infer a learner label.

Classroom observations are mixed:
- With a labeled diagram and oral follow-up, the learner distinguishes an observation from a proposed cause and points out that shade and watering changed together.
- On a dense written prompt, the learner leaves the causal justification incomplete. The teacher has not yet checked whether the directions were understood.
- A familiar bilingual glossary is routinely available in instruction. The learner sometimes uses it to interpret directions; it supplies no scientific conclusion.
- The team has documented a persistent additional concern across linguistically appropriate supported observations and has reason to suspect a disability. The packet does not supply enough information to diagnose it. A colleague proposes waiting until English is fluent before evaluating the concern.

Another colleague proposes using the Overall score alone to remove supports, giving a lower-level matching task as the science assessment, and introducing an unfamiliar dictionary only on the next state-test day.

Prepare a reasoned assessment and consultation plan:
1. Distinguish English language proficiency evidence from the science construct. Explain what the domain pattern suggests investigating and what it cannot establish about content ability, readiness, disability or identity. Explain why an Overall-only decision would be insufficient even if the composite were available.
2. Design a low-linguistic-load formative check that preserves the comparison/causal-uncertainty target. State the content criterion and the separate language observations. Explain what would change if the target instead included an extended written argument.
3. Distinguish the familiar classroom glossary from replacing the science standard with matching. Explain routine use, annual review as proficiency grows and why an unfamiliar test-day-only tool is problematic. For any actual MCAS use, state what current eligibility and administration rules must still be checked; do not provide code tables or claim classroom use alone authorizes a state-test support.
4. Use SEM/confidence-band humility to explain the limits of one administration. Identify additional evidence or report details you would seek and how they could change the plan. Do not make up confidence intervals, conversions, growth rates or numerical Massachusetts exit thresholds. Explain why a comparison spanning the 2025-2026 scale reset needs the guide's new-baseline rule.
5. Respond to the evaluation-delay proposal. Describe continued language support and domain-aware, culturally and linguistically appropriate monitoring alongside a warranted evaluation; do not require fluency first, prescribe an invented waiting period or diagnose from the scores.
6. State an observable content goal, a language goal and a monitoring decision with an explicit uncertainty. Identify one plausible alternative explanation for incomplete written work and a way to investigate it without assigning a culture trait or fixed capacity.

Use S1's assessment-purpose/high-content rule, S2's inapplicable uses, S7's dual-error and monitoring guidance, S9's domain/composite/SEM limits and S10's routine-use/review principles. This case requires judgment about evidence and construct preservation, not a single score-based answer. Individual evaluation, current state-test eligibility, full psychometrics and reclassification decisions remain outside its scope.

Review boundary: judge the reasoning, use of evidence, tradeoffs and uncertainty through a real human action. There is no single required plan or keyword list. Keywords, completion, an unfamiliar tag or agreement with an example establish neither an authoritative judgment nor independent transfer evidence or mastery. Source-checked content denotes model wording comparison only, not human review. Do not infer ability, disability, culture traits or trauma from language background.

cards.front: Which two standards sources guide sheltered content and language instruction together?
cards.back: The subject-area Frameworks and WIDA Standards guide instruction in tandem: preserve the content goal while planning the academic language needed to engage with it.

cards.front: Does accessible SCI replace dedicated ESL, and should ESL remove learners from core SEI content?
cards.back: SCI and content accessibility alone do not provide enough dedicated language focus. Maintain dedicated ESL without removing EL students from core SEI content instruction.

cards.front: What should a meaning-based analysis inspect at word/phrase, sentence and discourse dimensions?
cards.back: Inspect word/phrase precision and everyday, cross-disciplinary or technical choices; sentence grammatical complexity; and discourse meaning, cohesion and density across a text.

cards.front: How do sentence frames fit into academic-language instruction in Objective 0008?
cards.back: Frames are one practice alongside explicit vocabulary and language-structure instruction and inclusion in classroom academic discourse; they support participation rather than replacing it.

cards.front: Why inspect ACCESS domains instead of relying only on an Overall composite?
cards.back: A higher result in one language domain can inflate a composite and mask differences. Individual domain performance is more informative than a single composite score.

cards.front: What routine-use and review principles does the supplied MCAS manual give for EL accommodations?
cards.back: Do not use accommodations only for testing. Avoid unfamiliar bilingual dictionaries or glossaries, and examine and revise supports annually as English proficiency grows.
